query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 0.1 at.% carbon dopant in a refractory high-entropy alloy (such as a MoNbTaW-based system) followed by an optimized high-temperature heat treatment will trigger in situ formation of fine carbide precipitates that enhance high-temperature yield strength, while the minor addition preserves room-temperature ductility and does not significantly increase the alloy’s density.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaW or similar) without carbon doping, which exhibits high strength at elevated temperatures but has room-temperature brittleness and limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Add a trace amount of carbon (0.1 at.%) into the alloy composition to promote carbide formation during a subsequent high-temperature treatment.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied during alloy synthesis and followed by an optimized heat treatment at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) for carbide precipitation; mechanical properties are then evaluated under jet-turbine-like high-temperature loading as well as at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formed nanoscale carbides (e.g., Ta3C and Nb3C) dispersed within the matrix serve as obstacles to dislocation motion at high temperature.
generation.mechanism: The formation of fine carbide precipitates provides precipitation strengthening at elevated temperatures without substantially altering the alloy’s density or negatively affecting the room-temperature microstructure, thereby preserving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature conditions, the doped alloy is expected to exhibit an increased yield strength (compared to the undoped baseline) due to the carbide reinforcement, while its room-temperature yield strength and ductility remain comparable to those of the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: The same refractory HEA processed identically but without the carbon addition.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits are expected to hold in the temperature range relevant for jet turbine applications (approximately 800–1000 °C) and may not extend to temperatures far outside this range; results are also contingent on the optimized heat treatment facilitating carbide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of yield strength improvement under high-temperature conditions is uncertain, as is the precise distribution and size of the carbide precipitates; further investigation is required to ensure that room-temperature ductility is unaffected.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples with identical compositions and processing histories, with one set doped with 0.1 at.% carbon and the other serving as a control. Subject both sets to the same high-temperature heat treatment (e.g., 800–1000 °C) to promote any carbide formation. Conduct mechanical testing at high temperatures (simulating jet turbine operating conditions) to measure yield strength and at room temperature to assess ductility.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM or XRD) to confirm carbide formation and phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in high-temperature yield strength compared to the undoped samples, or if the room-temperature mechanical performance is degraded (e.g., reduced ductility), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are considered as a new class of advanced metallic materials, are drawing increasing attention because of their promising properties [,,], such as high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures [,], exceptional ductility [], and toughness []. HEAs were initially defined as alloys containing five or more elements with equal or near-equal concentrations [], while the later studies expended HEAs to include minor elements []. Many studies on HEAs were motivated by the possibility that properties may be tunable based on the elements contained in the HEAs. For example, Al-based HEAs [,,,] were studied for application on aircraft engines and nuclear reactors because of their low densities. On the other hand, because of the high melting temperature and high hardness of W and Re, HEAs that contained W or Re were expected to maintain advanced mechanical properties for high-temperature applications [,].

reading.lever: Introduce trace (0.1 at.%) carbon doping to trigger in situ carbide formation during optimized high-temperature treatment.
reading.why: This intervention uses a lightweight compositional change proven in refractory HEAs to generate strengthening carbides without compromising room-temperature performance or increasing density.
